recent_posts.title: A PHP license change is imminent
recent_posts.summary: PHP is moving toward replacing its two existing licenses (PHP v3.01 and Zend v2.0) with the BSD three-clause license. Led by Ben Ramsey, the effort has been in discussion since July 2025 and is now in a community vote through April 4, 2026. The change addresses long-standing confusion around the PHP Group not being a legal entity, OSI non-approval of PHP License 3.01, and GPL incompatibility issues. Ramsey secured approval from all PHP Group members and Perforce Software (current Zend owner), and argues that individual contributors do not need to consent since the new license does not reduce any rights they previously granted. The RFC also proposes removing build-time linking options for GPLv3 libraries (GNU Readline and GDBM) to simplify packaging. Early voting shows 47 in favor and 2 abstentions.

recent_posts.title: Building a programming language from scratch including parser, IR, and AArch64 JIT compiler
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their experience building a custom programming language called pslang from scratch, motivated by game modding needs. The post covers the language's design decisions including indentation-based scoping, a static nominal type system with 13 primitive types, arrays, pointers, and structs. It details the implementation stack: a Bison-based parser, a tree-walking interpreter, an IR similar to SSA, and a JIT compiler targeting AArch64. The author discusses challenges like handling indentation in a context-free grammar, encoding 32-bit constants in AArch64 instructions, and struct representation in IR. Future plans include a register allocator, generics, operator overloading, RAII or linear types for resource management, modules, and a standard library.

recent_posts.title: GitHub - scosman/cursed_browser: A web browser with no rendering engine — the VLM reads the HTML and hallucinates the page.
recent_posts.summary: Cursed Browser is a satirical open-source project that replaces a traditional browser rendering engine with a Visual Language Model (VLM). Instead of parsing HTML and CSS conventionally, it feeds the raw HTML to an LLM which then 'hallucinates' what the page should look like. Side-by-side comparisons with Safari show wildly different but creative results. The project includes a tongue-in-cheek roadmap featuring a fictional $200M pre-seed round for a V2 that would generate a new browser engine from scratch on every page load.

recent_posts.title: How an HTTP header caused time.gov to skew from UTC
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into why time.gov displayed inaccurate clock offsets. The root cause was the HTTP `Connection: close` header, which forced browsers to create a new TCP+TLS connection for every request. The JavaScript timing code assumed a single network round-trip (like NTP), but actually measured three, introducing a full round-trip worth of error. NIST fixed the issue around April 24th by switching to `keep-alive`. The author also proposes using the `PerformanceResourceTiming` API for more precise measurement of just the HTTP layer, and provides a client-side patch demonstrating the improvement.

recent_posts.title: Principia Softwarica
recent_posts.summary: Principia Softwarica is a book series that explains how fundamental system programs work by presenting fully annotated source code from Plan 9 from Bell Labs. Using literate programming, each book covers a core program — kernel, shell, compiler, linker, editor, debugger — with a target ratio of one line of explanation per line of code. Plan 9 was chosen because its entire codebase fits in ~183K lines, making it feasible to explain every line. The series argues that understanding the real full stack (compiler, linker, kernel, system calls) is increasingly critical as AI tools handle routine coding tasks. Several Plan 9 concepts underpin modern software: UTF-8, /proc, Linux namespaces (Docker), Go's goroutines, and WSL2's 9P protocol. OCaml ports of the programs are also available as a companion project called XIX.

recent_posts.title: Cryptographic Module Validation Program
recent_posts.summary: The Go Cryptographic Module has received validation under the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), a joint effort between NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. The module is a software library providing cryptographic functionality to the Go standard library and other Go applications. It operates in an approved mode with noted caveats around minimum strength assurances for generated and externally loaded security-sensitive parameters (SSPs) such as keys.

recent_posts.title: krabby: making a fast Rust compiler
recent_posts.summary: Krabby is a from-scratch Rust compiler implementation built with performance as the primary goal. The author argues that meaningful compilation speed improvements in rustc are now blocked by architectural constraints in a large, stability-focused codebase. Krabby takes a blank-slate approach, allowing every component to be designed with all others in mind, with the hope of uncovering large-scale architectural optimizations impossible in rustc. The project is hosted on Codeberg and is in early stages, with the author acknowledging the massive scope and uncertainty of completion.

recent_posts.title: One week of view_types
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares early thoughts after one week of working on the view_types feature for Rust (rust-lang/rust#155938). The post explores syntax considerations for view types applied to both immutable and mutable borrows, the possibility of supporting view types for owned values T in addition to &T (enabling partially initialized data and type-checked builder patterns without generic state tracking), challenges around expressing different lifetimes for different fields, and the author's evolving opinion on the proposed syntax. The author notes that extended exposure to a syntax tends to normalize it, drawing a parallel to their experience with let_else.

recent_posts.title: Why AI coding agents are not accelerating product quality at the frontier
recent_posts.summary: AI coding agents like Claude Code are producing a k-shaped productivity curve: senior engineers gain meaningfully while junior engineers stagnate or regress. Respected builders like David Cramer (Sentry) and Karri Saarinen (Linear) observe that agentic coding generates bloat, poor incremental development, and slop test generation rather than genuine product improvement. The key argument: if Claude Code truly compounded engineering velocity, Anthropic's 7-month head start should have made competitors irrelevant — but Codex, Cursor, and others remain competitive, proving the bottleneck was never code production speed. Lines of code are a cost, not an asset. The real constraint at the product frontier is taste — the ability to build less, compress complexity, and generate ideas that make users care. Coding agents help get 0-to-1 products to a baseline faster (the 'Camry' tier), but they don't help frontier teams build better products; they just make codebases bigger faster.

recent_posts.title: How AI slop is degrading online developer communities
recent_posts.summary: A developer argues that AI-generated content ("AI slop") is degrading online communities by flooding them with low-effort, thoughtless contributions. The author distinguishes between building *with* AI (using it as a tool while applying human judgment) versus letting AI generate content wholesale and spamming it everywhere. Key points include: the asymmetry of effort between producing and refuting low-quality content, the importance of respecting community norms before sharing, and the risk that unchecked AI slop will drive genuine community members away. The author urges developers to ask whether their AI-assisted work genuinely contributes value before sharing it broadly.

top_posts.title: A 15 second coding test to filter job applicants
top_posts.summary: A former CTO shares a simple coding screening question used to filter job applicants. The test presents basic code logic that qualified developers can solve mentally in seconds, while unqualified candidates resort to copy-pasting into interpreters or AI tools. The question includes a hidden character that produces different results when copy-pasted versus solved manually. Results showed 50% of applicants used automated tools, 47% answered correctly, and 3% answered incorrectly, effectively halving the candidate pool requiring deeper review.

top_posts.title: Replacing Redis with PostgreSQL for caching and background jobs
top_posts.summary: PostgreSQL can replace Redis for caching, pub/sub, job queues, and sessions using UNLOGGED tables, LISTEN/NOTIFY, SKIP LOCKED, and JSONB. While PostgreSQL is 50-158% slower per operation (0.1-1ms difference), it eliminates network hops between databases, reduces infrastructure costs by ~$100/month, simplifies operations, and guarantees transactional consistency. The approach works best for small-to-medium apps with simple caching needs but isn't suitable for high-throughput scenarios (100k+ ops/sec) or applications requiring Redis-specific data structures like sorted sets or HyperLogLog.

top_posts.title: DoomPDF
top_posts.summary: DoomPDF is a unique adaptation of the classic Doom game that executes within a PDF file, compatible exclusively with Chromium-based browsers. The source code is available on GitHub.

top_posts.title: Why there’s no European Google?
top_posts.summary: Europe hasn't produced tech giants like Google or Facebook, but has created fundamental infrastructure that powers the modern internet. The World Wide Web (HTTP/HTML), Linux, Git, Mastodon, VLC, and LibreOffice are all European inventions released as open source common goods rather than privatized for profit. European success is measured by long-term contribution to humanity rather than short-term wealth creation, with technologies designed to benefit everyone through copyleft licensing. This approach has produced lasting infrastructure that will outlive any individual company.
